new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (ya 'house', 'ya.ne 'my house', ya.'ne.mo 'in my house', ko.ndo.wo.'te.to 'we hold you'); secondary stress, rarely audible, on every second syllable leftward from the primary (4th, 6th from the end). Falling vowel sequences [-high][+high] (ou, əu, əi) count as one syllable peak with a single stress on the first vowel; other vowel sequences count as two peaks (sec. 2.5.2, p. 12-13).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress, though seldom present, is placed on syllables which are fourth from the end, sixth from the end, etc.' (p. 10) -- i.e. alternating leftward from the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 11: 'This general rule of stress placement is sometimes violated according to the intonation patterns of the phrase. That is, when the phrase has the intonation pattern of an interrogatory, the stress of the final word is on the final syllable rather than the penultimate. Stress is also often found on the final syllable of a root which is [+nasal] (see §2.4.3).' Examples pa.'rá 'big', pa.'rá.mi 'very big', pa.'rá.mi.mo 'on the very big one' (nasalised final root vowel keeps stress even under suffixation).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule (examples are inflected verb forms and case-suffixed nouns, stress recomputed on the whole word); phrase-final interrogative intonation can shift the last word's stress to the final syllable; author notes stress is used to disambiguate word division. No tone; nasalisation is a suprasegmental feature of roots/suffixes (sec. 2.4.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Iyo, the language formerly listed as Nahu [nca] (Minter 2009 sec. 1.2: name changed from 'Nahu' to 'Iyo', the word for 'yes', by community agreement); sec. 1.3 reports no distinct dialect boundaries, only village-level lexical differences (Nahu 1, Nahu 2, Rai Coast areas). Single glottocode iyoo1238; no dialect mismatch. The OPD header places the language in Saidor District, Madang Province (Gusap-Mot, Finisterre-Huon).

new_statements.relation_note: Same penultimate rule and secondary-stress statement as the catalog record (penultimate stress) and the existing statement, which was taken from this very section; the [+nasal]-root final-stress exception is a lexical/morphological refinement the catalog rule string does not encode.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; secondary stress (rarely realised) on every second syllable leftward from the primary (4th, 6th.. from the end). Examples: 'ya.ne 'my house', ya.'ne.mo 'in my house', ko.ndo.wo.'te.to 'we hold you'. In vowel sequences, a [-high][+high] sequence (ou, au, ai) counts as one syllable peak with stress on the first vowel; other sequences count as two peaks.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'Secondary stress, though seldom present, is placed on syllables which are fourth from the end, sixth from the end, etc.' (alternating leftward from the penult).
new_statements.exceptions: Two: (a) phrase-final word under yes/no-interrogative intonation takes final rather than penultimate stress; (b) roots carrying the lexical [+nasal] feature often stress their final syllable (pa.'ra 'big', pa.'ra.mi 'very big', pa.'ra.mi.mo 'on the very big one'). Also notes that apparent first- or third-syllable stress is usually resolved by re-dividing the word.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1998 manuscript uses the older language name 'Nahu' (Trans-New Guinea, Finisterre-Huon stock, Gusap-Mot family, 5,400+ speakers, Madang Province); the 2009 sketch uses 'Iyo'. Both describe the same language (Glottolog iyoo1238, ISO nca); no dialect is singled out in the stress sections.

new_statements.quote: Stress is very predictable in Nahu. The general rule is that the penultimate syllable has primary stress. Secondary stress, if present, is regularly placed on syllables which are fourth from the end, sixth from the end, etc. Stress placement can often be used to disambiguate word division; ie., a word with apparent stress on the first or third syllable can often be acceptably divided to conform to the general pattern. This general rule of stress placement is sometimes violated according to the intonation patterns of the phrase. That is, when the phrase has the intonation pattern of an interrogatory the stress of the final word is on the final syllable rather than the penultimate. Stress is also often found on the final syllable of a root which is [+nasal] (see Nasalisation below).

new_statements.relation_note: Verbatim precursor of the 2009 sketch sec. 2.4.1 (this ms. is cited there as Minter 1998a); same penultimate placement, same alternating secondary stress, same two exceptions. Adds the explicit statement that the language has no phonemic tone or length. The 1998 text calls the language 'Nahu' (the older name for Iyo, same language, 5,400+ speakers, Madang Province).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable; secondary stress, when present, regularly on the 4th, 6th.. syllable from the end. No phonemic tone or length. Vowel sequences [-high][+high] (ou, au, ai) form one syllable peak stressed on the first vowel; other sequences form two peaks. The nasalisation section adds that nasalised vowels were first thought to be confined to final stressed syllables but occur in unstressed syllables too (examples with primary stress marks: [»kAmA] 'not', [ku»si‚] 'bamboo').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'Secondary stress, if present, is regularly placed on syllables which are fourth from the end, sixth from the end, etc.'
new_statements.exceptions: Same two as the 2009 sketch: final stress on the last word of a phrase with interrogative intonation, and final stress often on [+nasal] roots. Also states 'There is no phonemic tone or lengthening in Nahu' (printed p. 5).
new_statements.identity_note: The 1998 manuscript uses the older language name 'Nahu' (Trans-New Guinea, Finisterre-Huon stock, Gusap-Mot family, 5,400+ speakers, Madang Province); the 2009 sketch uses 'Iyo'. Both describe the same language (Glottolog iyoo1238, ISO nca); no dialect is singled out in the stress sections.
